title: Accounting Policies
outcomes: Explain what accounting policies are and why no single set suits every enterprise.
Apply prudence, substance over form and materiality in selecting accounting policies, and explain why disclosure cannot cure a wrong treatment.
State when a change in accounting policy is permitted and quantify the effect of a change on profit and assets.

meta.exam_tip: Two lists to learn cold: selection — prudence, substance over form, materiality; change — statute/Accounting Standard or more appropriate presentation. Practise one FIFO vs weighted-average effect computation.

concepts.title: What accounting policies are
body: Accounting policies are the particular accounting principles an enterprise picks, together with the methods it uses to apply them, in preparing and presenting its financial statements. They rest on the concepts, principles and conventions of Unit 2.

There is no single list of policies that suits every enterprise in every situation: businesses work in varied and complex conditions, so management has to use careful judgement to choose the policy that fits its circumstances. ICAI, with the government, regulators and progressive managements, has been narrowing the range of acceptable policies through Accounting Standards and Guidance Notes.

Areas where different policies are often found include valuation of inventories and valuation of investments (the list is illustrative, not exhaustive — depreciation is another familiar example). For instance, an enterprise holding shares may value them using FIFO or the average method; the method chosen is its accounting policy.
concepts.analogy: Two cooks follow the same recipe principle ("cook till done") but choose different methods — oven or stove. The method each picks, and sticks to, is like an accounting policy.
concepts.work: Every annual report begins its notes with "Significant accounting policies". Analysts and auditors read it first, because the same transactions can give different profits under different policies.

concepts.title: Selecting accounting policies
body: The choice of policy is an important management decision: it affects both the measured performance and the financial position. An inappropriate policy can understate or overstate both, so policies must be chosen with care, looking at their effect from the angle of the various users.

Three major considerations govern selection and application: prudence, substance over form and materiality. The aim is that the financial statements present the position in the balance sheet and the result in the profit and loss account truly and fairly.

Typical policy statements: inventories valued at cost, except finished goods at the lower of cost and market value and by-products at net realisable value; long-term investments valued at acquisition cost with provision for permanent fall in value where necessary.
Disclosure of the policy adopted is always necessary — but disclosure cannot cure a wrong or inappropriate treatment. A wrong policy must be corrected, not merely disclosed.

head: Consideration
What it means when choosing a policy
Example
rows: Under uncertainty, choose the treatment that does not overstate assets or income, without creating secret reserves
Finished goods valued at lower of cost and net realisable value
Account for the economic reality, not merely the legal form
Asset whose risks and rewards have passed recorded as purchased although registration is pending
Policies should deal properly with every item that could influence users' decisions; trivial items may be treated simply
Small tools below a set limit expensed on purchase
blocks.title: Three considerations in selecting accounting policies

concepts.analogy: Telling a passenger "I drive on the wrong side of the road" (disclosure) does not make the journey safe; you have to drive on the correct side (correct policy).
concepts.work: When advising a new company, a CA drafts its accounting policies manual — inventory method, depreciation method and rates, revenue recognition — choosing options that are prudent, reflect substance and are consistent with Accounting Standards.

concepts.title: Changing an accounting policy
body: A change in accounting policy should be made only if (a) it is required by a statute or for compliance with an Accounting Standard, or (b) the change would result in a more appropriate presentation of the financial statements.

A change may materially affect items in the financial statements — for example, switching the inventory cost formula from weighted average to FIFO, starting to capitalise interest that was earlier expensed, or starting to include a share of interest or production overheads in inventory. Each can raise or lower the net profit.

Unless the effect of the change is quantified, users cannot compare the figures with those of earlier years. Therefore the effect of the change on assets, liabilities and profit or loss must be worked out and disclosed.
concepts.analogy: If a cricket board changes the size of the boundary mid-season, it must tell everyone how many extra sixes that produced — otherwise run totals cannot be compared with last season.
concepts.work: When a client changes its inventory method, the auditor checks the reason (standard, law or better presentation — not profit management), recalculates the effect and verifies the disclosure in the notes.

illustrations.title: Weighted average to FIFO — quantifying the effect
illustrations.q: Nova Electricals had no opening inventory on 1 April 2026. It bought 1,000 units at ₹50 in April, 1,500 units at ₹56 in July and 1,500 units at ₹60 in December, and sold 3,000 units at ₹90 each. Until now it used the weighted average cost formula (periodic). It decides to change to FIFO because it believes this gives a more appropriate presentation. Compute the gross profit under both formulas and the effect of the change that must be disclosed.

solution.title: Weighted average
solution.text: Total cost 50,000 + 84,000 + 90,000 = ₹2,24,000 for 4,000 units → ₹56 per unit. Closing inventory 1,000 × 56 = ₹56,000.

solution.title: FIFO
solution.text: The earliest units are sold first, so the 1,000 units left come from the December lot at ₹60: closing inventory ₹60,000.

head: Particulars
Weighted average (₹)
FIFO (₹)
solution.title: Effect of changing the cost formula — Nova Electricals, 2026-27

solution.text: Effect of the change: closing inventory and gross profit are higher by ₹4,000 under FIFO. The note on accounting policies must state the change, the reason and this effect.

checks.label: Increase in profit due to the change

illustrations.q: Omkar Foods valued its closing inventory of 2,000 units of finished goods at material and labour cost of ₹150 per unit. From 2026-27 it decides to include production overheads of ₹30 per unit, believing that this gives a more appropriate presentation. Show the effect of the change.

Working

The change is permitted because it gives a more appropriate presentation; the effect must be quantified and disclosed so that this year's profit can be compared fairly with last year's.

illustrations.title: Is the change allowed?
illustrations.q: State whether each proposed change in accounting policy is acceptable: (1) a company changes its depreciation method because a newly notified Accounting Standard requires it; (2) a company switches its inventory formula in a bad year only to report a higher profit; (3) a company starts valuing by-products at net realisable value because it gives a more appropriate presentation; (4) a company keeps a wrong policy but explains it fully in the notes.

jobs.title: A client wants to "improve" profit
jobs.role: Practising CA finalising a private company's accounts
jobs.situation: Sales have fallen. The managing director suggests changing the depreciation method from written-down value to straight-line this year "to show better profit to the bank".
steps: Explain the permitted grounds for a change: a statute, an Accounting Standard, or a more appropriate presentation.
Ask whether the pattern in which the assets' benefits are consumed has genuinely changed; if not, the reason given is profit management.
If a change is justified, compute its effect on depreciation, profit and asset values and disclose it.
Explain that the bank will read the policy note — an unexplained jump in profit from a policy change damages credibility.
jobs.takeaway: Policies are chosen for a true and fair view, not for a target profit. Every change must be justified and its effect disclosed.
jobs.think: If the change were justified, why must its effect be quantified?
jobs.answer: Without the figure, users cannot tell how much of the change in profit came from operations and how much from the new policy, so comparison with earlier years would mislead.

jobs.title: Drafting the policy note for a new business
jobs.role: Accounts manager at a start-up trading company
jobs.situation: The company's first annual accounts are due. The auditor asks for a draft "significant accounting policies" note.
steps: List the material areas: revenue recognition, inventory valuation (cost formula, lower of cost and net realisable value), depreciation (method and rates), investments, foreign currency.
For each, choose a policy that is prudent, reflects substance over form and follows the applicable Accounting Standard.
Write each policy in plain words so that a reader with reasonable business knowledge can understand it.
Agree the note with the auditor; future years must follow it consistently.
jobs.takeaway: The first set of policies becomes the benchmark for consistency in every later year — choose carefully.

options: The particular accounting principles chosen by an enterprise and the methods it uses to apply them
The rules framed by the Income-tax Department
The internal control procedures of a business
The auditor's report on the financial statements
mcqs.explain: Accounting policies are the specific accounting principles an enterprise chooses, together with the methods of applying them, when preparing and presenting its financial statements — for example, FIFO for inventory or straight-line depreciation. The tempting option, rules framed by the Income-tax Department, confuses tax computation rules with accounting choices; tax rules decide taxable income, not how accounts are presented. In practice: the first note in every Indian company's annual report is 'Significant Accounting Policies'.

mcqs.q: The three major considerations governing the selection of accounting policies are:
options: Prudence, substance over form and materiality
mcqs.explain: The three major considerations in selecting accounting policies are prudence, substance over form and materiality. The trap is going concern, consistency and accrual — these are the fundamental accounting assumptions that are presumed to be followed, not the considerations used to choose between alternative policies. Relevance, reliability and comparability are qualitative characteristics of statements. In practice: when choosing a revenue recognition policy, a finance team considers prudence and economic substance, not just legal form.

mcqs.q: A change in accounting policy should be made:
options: If required by statute or an Accounting Standard, or for a more appropriate presentation
mcqs.explain: A change in accounting policy is allowed only if a statute requires it, an Accounting Standard requires it, or the change gives a more appropriate presentation of the financial statements. The tempting option, 'whenever profits fall', describes profit management, which is exactly what the consistency convention guards against. Changing on a fixed timetable or with a new auditor has no basis. In practice: companies moving to Ind AS changed many policies because the new standards required it.

mcqs.q: A company has followed an inappropriate accounting treatment but has disclosed it fully in the notes. Which statement is correct?
options: Disclosure cannot rectify a wrong or inappropriate treatment
Full disclosure makes the treatment acceptable
The treatment becomes correct after auditor approval
mcqs.explain: Disclosure of accounting policies is always required, but disclosure cannot rectify a wrong or inappropriate treatment; the treatment itself must be correct. The tempting option, 'full disclosure makes the treatment acceptable', is the classic misconception — a note explaining an error is still an error. Auditor approval does not cure it either. In practice: if a company wrongly capitalises routine expenses, a statutory auditor will qualify the report even if the note describes the policy clearly.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of an area where different accounting policies are commonly found?
mcqs.explain: Different accounting policies are commonly found where accounting standards allow more than one acceptable method, and valuation of inventories is a standard example (FIFO or weighted average), along with depreciation and valuation of investments. The tempting options — a cash sale, salary payment or posting — are routine recording steps with only one correct treatment, so no policy choice arises. In practice: two FMCG companies may report different profits partly because one uses FIFO and the other weighted average.

mcqs.q: Closing inventory under weighted average is ₹84,000 and under FIFO ₹91,500. If a company changes from weighted average to FIFO, profit for the year will:
mcqs.explain: Closing inventory reduces cost of goods sold. A higher closing inventory under FIFO (₹91,500 instead of ₹84,000) lowers cost of goods sold by ₹7,500 and therefore increases profit by ₹91,500 − ₹84,000 = ₹7,500. The tempting option, 'decrease by ₹7,500', reverses the link between closing inventory and profit. In practice: when prices are rising, FIFO usually shows higher inventory and profit than weighted average, which is why such a change must be justified and its effect disclosed.

mcqs.q: Purchases: 400 units @ ₹100 and 600 units @ ₹110; 700 units sold; no opening inventory. Closing inventory under FIFO is:
mcqs.explain: Under FIFO, the earliest goods are treated as sold first. The 700 units sold use up all 400 units at ₹100 and 300 of the ₹110 lot, so the 300 units left are from the latest lot: 300 × ₹110 = ₹33,000. The tempting ₹31,800 is the weighted average figure (300 × ₹106), not FIFO. In practice: FIFO often matches the physical flow of goods in businesses such as pharmaceuticals and groceries, where older stock must be sold first.

mcqs.q: Same data: 400 units @ ₹100 and 600 units @ ₹110; 700 units sold. Closing inventory under the weighted average method (periodic) is:
mcqs.explain: Under the periodic weighted average method, average cost = total cost ÷ total units = (₹40,000 + ₹66,000) ÷ 1,000 = ₹106 per unit, so closing inventory = 300 × ₹106 = ₹31,800. The tempting ₹33,000 values all 300 units at the latest price of ₹110, which is FIFO. A simple average of ₹105 would also be wrong, because the lots are of different sizes. In practice: many Indian manufacturers use weighted average costing in their ERP systems for raw materials.

mcqs.q: Closing inventory of 1,500 units was valued at ₹200 per unit. A new policy adds production overheads of ₹24 per unit. The increase in profit is:
mcqs.explain: Adding production overheads of ₹24 per unit raises closing inventory by 1,500 × ₹24 = ₹36,000. Higher closing inventory means lower cost of goods sold, so profit rises by ₹36,000 in the year of change. The tempting ₹3,36,000 is the new total inventory value (1,500 × ₹224), not the change in profit. In practice: when a company starts absorbing overheads into inventory, as AS 2 requires, it must disclose the effect of this change on the year's profit.

mcqs.q: Why must the effect of a change in accounting policy be quantified?
options: So that users can compare the statements with earlier periods
To avoid preparing a cash flow statement
mcqs.explain: A change in policy alters reported profit even if business performance is unchanged. Quantifying its effect lets users separate the impact of the change from real performance and compare the current statements with earlier periods. The tempting option, 'because tax law prohibits changes', is false; tax law does not prohibit accounting policy changes. In practice: analysts reading a listed company's results look for the note quantifying any policy change before comparing year-on-year profit growth.

mcqs.q: Selecting an inappropriate accounting policy may lead to:
options: Overstatement or understatement of performance and financial position
mcqs.explain: The choice of accounting policy affects both the measured performance (profit) and the financial position (balance sheet), so an inappropriate policy can overstate or understate both. The tempting option, 'higher sales volume', confuses accounting with real business activity — a policy changes how results are reported, not what customers buy. In practice: overly aggressive revenue recognition policies have led to inflated profits in corporate frauds, which is why auditors scrutinise policy choices closely.

mcqs.q: Which body, working with the government and regulators, issues Accounting Standards and Guidance Notes that narrow down the choice of acceptable policies?
options: ICAI, along with the government and regulators
The Reserve Bank of India alone
mcqs.explain: The Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, working with the government, regulators and progressive managements, issues Accounting Standards and Guidance Notes that narrow the range of acceptable policies. The tempting option, the RBI alone, is a regulator for banks and NBFCs; it prescribes some norms for them but does not issue the general accounting standards. In practice: standards are formulated by ICAI's Accounting Standards Board and notified for companies by the Central Government.

It used the weighted average (periodic) formula and now changes to FIFO for a more appropriate presentation. model.text: Total cost ₹5,10,000 ÷ 6,000 = ₹85 per unit; closing inventory 1,500 × 85 = ₹1,27,500.

Effect: closing inventory and gross profit are higher by ₹7,500 under FIFO. The change is permitted because it is made for a more appropriate presentation; the change, its reason and its effect of ₹7,500 must be disclosed.

questions.q: When can an enterprise change its accounting policy? Why should the effect of the change be quantified? Give two examples of such changes.

model.text: A change in accounting policy should be made only when (a) it is required by a statute or for compliance with an Accounting Standard, or (b) it would result in a more appropriate presentation of the financial statements.

A change can materially increase or decrease profit and alter assets and liabilities. Unless its effect is quantified, users cannot compare the current figures with earlier periods or know how much of the change in profit is due to the policy rather than performance. So the effect on assets, liabilities and profit or loss is quantified and disclosed.

items: Changing the inventory cost formula from weighted average to FIFO.
Starting to include production overheads (or a share of interest) in the cost of inventory, or to capitalise interest that was earlier expensed.

remarks: Good answers keep the grounds to the two listed; adding "to increase profit" as a ground is a serious error.
mistakes: Saying a policy can never be changed.
Giving a change in an estimate (useful life) as a change in policy.
tips: Number the two grounds; write the reason for quantifying in one sentence.

summary: Accounting policies = specific principles + methods of applying them adopted by an enterprise for its financial statements.
No universal list; management judgement needed. ICAI narrows choices through Accounting Standards and Guidance Notes.
Selection: prudence, substance over form, materiality — aiming at a true and fair view.
Change only if required by statute/Accounting Standard or for a more appropriate presentation; quantify and disclose the effect.
Disclosure is always needed but cannot rectify a wrong treatment.
remember: Higher closing inventory after a change → higher profit by the same amount.
FIFO: closing stock from the latest lots; weighted average: total cost ÷ total units.
traps: Going concern, consistency, accrual are the fundamental assumptions — not the selection criteria.
A revision of useful life is a change in estimate, not a change in policy.
"To show higher profit" is never a valid reason for change.

points.pt: Example: weighted average to FIFO / overheads in inventory / capitalising interest

cases.title: Lotus Paints — a change of cost formula
cases.case: Lotus Paints had no opening inventory on 1 April 2026. It bought 500 tins at ₹400, 700 tins at ₹420 and 800 tins at ₹450 during the year, and 600 tins remained unsold on 31 March 2027. Until last year it used the weighted average formula. The finance director wants to switch to FIFO and argues that "it will lift profit, and anyway we will mention it in the notes".

mcqs.q: What is the closing inventory under the weighted average formula?
mcqs.explain: Weighted average cost = total cost ÷ total tins. Total cost = (500 × 400) + (700 × 420) + (800 × 450) = ₹8,54,000 for 2,000 tins, so average = ₹427. Closing inventory = 600 × ₹427 = ₹2,56,200. The tempting ₹2,52,000 uses a simple average of the three prices (₹420), ignoring the different quantities. In practice: paint and chemical manufacturers often use weighted average because tins from different lots are physically mixed in the warehouse.

mcqs.q: What is the closing inventory under FIFO?
mcqs.explain: Under FIFO the oldest tins are treated as sold first, so the 600 tins left are from the latest purchase of 800 tins at ₹450: 600 × ₹450 = ₹2,70,000. The tempting ₹2,56,200 is the weighted average figure. When prices are rising, FIFO leaves the most recent, higher-cost goods in inventory. In practice: during periods of rising input costs, FIFO inventory figures are closer to current replacement cost than weighted average figures.

mcqs.q: By how much will profit change if FIFO is adopted?
mcqs.explain: Closing inventory reduces cost of goods sold. FIFO inventory ₹2,70,000 − weighted average inventory ₹2,56,200 = ₹13,800 higher inventory, so cost of goods sold falls and profit rises by ₹13,800. The tempting option, a decrease of ₹13,800, reverses the link: higher closing inventory raises profit, not lowers it. In practice: this effect would reverse in the following year when the higher opening inventory flows into cost of goods sold.

options: A change is allowed only for a statute, a standard or a more appropriate presentation — not to lift profit; disclosure does not cure an improper change
Any change is fine if it is mentioned in the notes
Changes are never allowed once a policy is chosen
The change is allowed because FIFO always gives higher profit
mcqs.explain: A change in accounting policy is allowed only if a statute or Accounting Standard requires it or the change gives a more appropriate presentation. Lifting profit is not a valid ground, and disclosure does not cure an improper change. The tempting option says any change is fine if noted — that confuses disclosure with justification. If a valid ground exists, the effect must be quantified and disclosed. In practice: auditors challenge policy changes made near year end that conveniently improve profit.
